Steam, Emacs, VLC, LaTeX, Adobe Reader, Spotify (technically counts, right?)

• Vim: It's an extensible, command-driven text editor with a GUI front-end called GVim. Maybe you'd prefer Emacs. Maybe you'd prefer anything else. To each their own.

  • Krita: Drawing and painting application. Basic raster-based animation was just implemented aspiring to be fully featured. Right now their mailing list is exploding with build statuses. They look like they're busy hauling everything to Qt 5 at the moment.

  • Ardour: Digital audio workstation. Supported on Linux and OS X, although can compile and work on Windows, just not supported. Requires JACK to run.

  • JACK: Low-latency audio server. Supported on all platforms. You can route any JACK-compliant application through it and make some crazy routings. Great for pod-casting and general real-time audio work. It's like a beefed up ReWire. Bitwig Studio actually uses JACK instead of ReWire.

  • LLVM: For developers. It's an MIT-style licensed compiler infrastructure, aiming to be the universal compiler. You don't necessarily use LLVM directly, you use a front-end for it, like clang (C compiler) or clang++ or what-have-you. Clang is gcc compatible and supports cross-compilation. On Windows it supports the MSVC ABI and also has a clang-cl binary to make it command-line compatible with cl.
